perspective:
I, Sara Manuelito, know:

- I am a Speech-Language Pathologist; Shirley Whiteplume is a nurse and a long-time colleague and close friend at our community health center.
- We attended the funeral of a mutual patient. I saw Shirley was somber and suspected she was deeply affected. I heard her say it had been tough, that she kept thinking if there was something more we could have done, and that it was hard to let go. I told her we did everything we could and should remember the good care and moments of joy we brought; she agreed.
- During a work coffee break, I brought up our treatment decisions because I sensed Shirley felt burdened by the outcome. She told me she felt responsible and wondered if pushing for a different approach might have helped. I said we made the best decisions with the information we had and that the burden was too heavy to carry alone. She appreciated it but said it was hard to accept.
- In a quiet office moment, I had noticed Shirley was reserved and minimally expressive. I told her it was okay to be open about her feelings. She said she was not sure she could and did not want to seem unprofessional or weak. I said expressing emotions does not make her weak and is healthy among friends. She said maybe I was right and she would try to be more open.
- Later, I felt my previous confrontation might have been too harsh. I apologized. Shirley said it was a bit much but she knew I meant well and appreciated the apology. I said I was there for her however she needed. She thanked me and said we should keep talking because it helps.
- After some time, I noticed Shirley seemed to be doing better and asked how she felt. She said she felt better thanks to our talks and my support. I offered to spend more time together outside work. She agreed and suggested planning something for the weekend.
